how-to-build-confidence-in-children:
Confidence cannot be praised into a child. It is a by-product of competence, and the attempts to install it directly tend to produce the opposite, which is why so much well-meant encouragement lands badly.

Where it actually comes from

A child becomes confident by doing difficult things and finding out they can. Not by being told they can. The belief has to be earned against reality, because a child knows the difference between an assessment and a compliment long before they can say so.

Which means the raw material of confidence is opportunity: real tasks, real difficulty, a genuine chance of failing, and nobody stepping in too early.

Why praise often works against it

Three ways, and the first is the most common.

Praise for being rather than doing. "You're so clever" names a category, and a category can be lost. Children praised for ability become more cautious, because the next hard thing threatens the label. Children praised for effort and strategy take on harder work.

Praise that does not match reality. Telling a child a mediocre drawing is wonderful teaches them that your assessments carry no information, which devalues the real ones.

Praise as a constant background. If everything is brilliant then nothing is, and the child starts performing for the reaction instead of attending to the task.

What to say instead

Notice specifically and without evaluating. "You kept going with that even when it was annoying." "You tried it a second way." "That bit at the end took you three attempts."

These do two things at once: they tell the child you were actually watching, and they point at the thing that is within their control.

Also useful, and underused: ask them what they think of it. A child who can evaluate their own work is not dependent on somebody else's verdict, which is what confidence actually consists of.

The thing that quietly destroys it

Doing things for them. Every task an adult takes over to save time is a message that they could not have managed it, and it is received.

This is hardest when a child is struggling in front of you, which is exactly when stepping in feels most like kindness. Sitting nearby and saying nothing is frequently the more useful act.

Rebuilding it once it has gone

A child who has decided they are bad at something will not be argued out of it. What works is evidence, gathered slowly.

Find something adjacent they can genuinely succeed at, and let them do it repeatedly until the success is undeniable to them. Keep the difficulty just above comfortable. Do not narrate the improvement too loudly, because a child who suspects they are being managed will discount the whole thing.

Expect it to take months. Beliefs about the self are formed slowly and revised slowly.

The aim is not a child who believes they are good at everything. It is a child who believes that difficulty is survivable and that they can get better at things, which is more durable and considerably more true.
how-to-help-a-shy-child:
Shyness is a temperament, not a fault, and roughly one child in five is born with a nervous system that reacts more strongly to unfamiliar things. That reaction is visible in infancy and it is largely stable, which means the goal cannot be to convert a shy child into an outgoing one.

The goal is a child who can do what they want to do despite the feeling. That is achievable, and the route to it is narrower than most advice suggests.

What makes it worse

Almost everything instinctive.

Pushing. Made to say hello, made to perform, made to join in. This raises the stakes of an already high-stakes moment and teaches that social situations come with a demand attached.

Speaking for them. The adult who answers on the child's behalf removes the practice and confirms that the child cannot manage it. This one is difficult because it is nearly automatic and because it is polite.

Labelling. "She's shy", said in front of them, hands the child an identity and an excuse in the same sentence. They will use it.

Rescuing. Removing every uncomfortable situation prevents the child ever discovering that discomfort passes.

What helps

Warn in advance. Who will be there, how long, what will happen, what they can do if they need a break. Most of a shy child's distress is uncertainty, and uncertainty is removable.

Arrive early. Joining two people is manageable; walking into twenty is not. This single change transforms parties for many children.

Give them a job. Handing round something, holding the door, looking after a younger cousin. A role removes the question of what to do with yourself, which is most of the difficulty.

One friend at a time. Depth rather than breadth. A shy child with two real friendships is doing fine and does not need a wider circle.

Let them watch first. Many cautious children observe for a long time and then join competently. That watching is not avoidance; it is how they gather enough information to act.

Practise the small things. Ordering their own food, asking a shopkeeper a question, paying. Tiny rehearsals with low stakes, repeated, build a genuine store of evidence.

The reframe worth holding

Cautious children tend to be observant, thoughtful and good at reading situations, precisely because they watch before acting. Those are not consolation prizes. A household that treats shyness as a defect to be corrected teaches a child that a fundamental part of them is wrong.

When it is more than temperament

Worth raising with someone if the child cannot speak at all in certain settings while speaking normally at home over months, if they are refusing school, if they have no friendships at all and want them, or if the anxiety is spreading into things that were previously fine.

Those patterns respond well to help, and early help is lighter than later help.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
questions-to-ask-kids-instead-of-how-was:
"How was school?" reliably produces "fine", and then everybody feels slightly disappointed. The problem is not the child. It is that the question asks for a summary of seven hours, which is a genuinely hard thing to produce on demand at the end of a tiring day.

Specific questions are answerable. Here are ones that work, and then the thing that matters more than any of them.

About the day's shape

  • Who did you sit with at lunch?
  • What was the most annoying part of today?
  • What made you laugh?
  • When were you bored?
  • Did anything happen that was unfair?

About people

  • Who was kind to somebody today?
  • Did anybody get in trouble? What for?
  • Who would you like to sit next to tomorrow?
  • Is there anybody you feel sorry for?

About the work

  • What was the hardest thing you had to do?
  • Did you learn anything you did not believe?
  • What did you get wrong today?
  • If you were the teacher, what would you have done differently?

Sideways, which often works best

  • Tell me one good thing and one bad thing.
  • What would you rate today out of ten, and what would have made it one point higher?
  • If today were a weather forecast, what was it?
  • What is something you know now that you did not know this morning?

The part that matters more than the question

When you ask. The moment a child comes out is the worst time. They are tired, hungry, and have been performing socially for hours. Feed them, let twenty minutes pass, and ask later.

Where you ask. Side by side beats face to face, every time. The car, a walk, washing up, driving somewhere. Children say considerably more when they are not being looked at, and adolescents say almost nothing when they are.

How you react to the first thing. The whole conversation is decided here. If a child mentions something small and gets a lecture, an interrogation or visible alarm, you have taught them what happens when they open a subject. If they get interest, they open another.

Ask one, not six. A list of questions is an interview, and children can tell. One question, a real pause, and a willingness to let the answer be short.

And say nothing sometimes

The most reliable way to get a child talking is to be available and unbusy, and to not ask anything at all. A great deal of what parents want to know arrives twenty minutes into a car journey, unprompted, after the questions have stopped.
how-to-encourage-children-to-talk-more:
Most children talk more when two things change, and neither is about asking better questions. The first is how long you wait. The second is what you do with the answer.

Wait longer than is comfortable

Adults typically leave about a second before filling a silence. Children frequently need several, and children who are tired, shy or still assembling the sentence need more.

Count to five silently after asking something. It will feel unbearable and a surprising amount will arrive in the fourth second. This is the single highest-value change available and it costs nothing.

Do not improve what they said

The instinct to correct grammar, supply the better word, or finish the sentence is strong and it is expensive. A child who is corrected mid-flow attends to the correction rather than the thing they were saying, and over time says less.

If you want to model the right form, repeat it back correctly as part of your reply, without comment. "I goed to the park." "You went to the park! Who was there?" The child hears the correct form and loses nothing.

Comment rather than question

A run of questions is an interview and children close down under it. Statements invite response without demanding it.

"That tower is taller than the last one." "I notice you did the red ones first." "I would not have thought of that."

Each of these leaves a space that a child can step into or not, which is quite different from a question, which requires an answer.

Go where they are already going

Ten minutes of genuine interest in the thing they are obsessed with does more than an hour of your chosen topic. This is tedious when the topic is a game you do not understand, and it is the price of the channel staying open at fourteen.

Talk side by side

Cooking, walking, driving, building, washing up. Shoulder to shoulder removes the pressure of being looked at, and for many children it is the difference between a conversation and an interrogation.

Narrate your own thinking

Children mirror the talk they hear. If the adults in a house think out loud, weigh things aloud, change their minds aloud, children do too. "I am trying to decide whether to do this now or later, because if I leave it we will be rushing." That is a model of reasoning, offered without a lesson attached.

What suppresses talking

Being tested. Correcting. Reacting strongly to the content. Finishing sentences. Asking questions you already know the answer to, which children spot instantly. And phones, which children read accurately as evidence of where attention actually is.

If a child talks very little

Some are simply quiet, and quiet is not a problem to be solved. Worth raising with somebody if there are few words by two, no two-word phrases by two and a half, speech that others cannot understand at four, a child who does not respond to their name, or speech that has gone backwards.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
